title: Isandro and the Parish
premise: When the coffin of Isandro Vey, founder of the river town of Parish, is found empty during a centennial exhumation, night-shift dispatcher August Okonkwo notices that three recent 'accidents' all involved people who claimed to have seen Isandro alive after his burial. Following dispatch logs, funeral records, and her own uncanny memory for voices, August traces a living witness the town insists is dead — Isandro's illegitimate daughter, hidden away in the parish poorhouse. The town's ruling families, whose fortunes rest on Isandro's death certificate, close ranks around her. In the flooded crypt beneath the church, August discovers Isandro never died at all: he faked his death to expose the embezzlement of the parish trust, and the 'accidents' were his heirs silencing witnesses. Confronting them with recorded testimony, she forces the truth into daylight, though not before the last heir tries to bury her alongside the secret.
about_author: Cyrus Marchetti is the pen name of a former small-town court reporter who spent a decade transcribing the quiet crimes of rural America before turning to fiction. He lives near a river town much like Parish and still keeps the dispatch scanner on at night.

chapters.title: The Empty Box
chapters.summary: Third-person limited, August's POV. During the centennial exhumation, the coffin lid comes up light; inside there is only river silt and a brass nameplate polished by hands. August, attending out of habit rather than grief, notices the undertaker's face go gray. Emotional beat: quiet recognition that something everyone treats as ceremony has just become evidence.

chapters.title: Night Shift Frequencies
chapters.summary: August's POV. Back at the dispatch office, August cross-references three past 'accidents' — a drowned sexton, a burned archivist, a fall from the viaduct — against call logs and finds each victim had called a cab to the cemetery the week before dying. Emotional beat: the cold thrill of a pattern snapping into focus.

chapters.title: What the Town Remembers
chapters.summary: August interviews the historical society, where the Vey family matriarch, Cordelia, charmingly deflects every question about Isandro's final year. A junior archivist slips August a photograph showing Isandro with an unknown young woman dated after his death. Emotional beat: the unease of polite power closing like a door.

chapters.title: The Poorhouse Ledger
chapters.summary: August's POV. In county records she finds a 1962 admission entry: an infant girl, surname Vey, delivered to the parish poorhouse by a man paid in cash. The ledger page has been razored out — but August remembers the carbon copy from a voice on the phone years ago. Emotional beat: memory as an instrument sharper than paper.

chapters.title: Accident Number Four
chapters.summary: A taxi driver who once drove the young woman to the bus depot dies when his cab goes into the river. August had spoken to him hours earlier; his last words were a street address. Police rule it accidental. Emotional beat: grief curdling into resolve — she is no longer observing the pattern, she is inside it.

chapters.title: Cordelia's Tea
chapters.summary: Cordelia Vey invites August for tea, offering help while probing exactly what August knows. She mentions, too casually, that the witness everyone swears is dead — 'poor Ruthie' — died decades ago. August recognizes the name from the ledger. Emotional beat: a duel fought entirely in courtesies.

chapters.title: Ruthie
chapters.summary: August traces Ruthie Vey to a care facility two counties over, where a woman in her sixties lives under another name, terrified of visitors. Ruthie saw her father alive in the flooded crypt in 1971 and has been hiding ever since. Emotional beat: fear passed down like inheritance.

chapters.title: The Trust
chapters.summary: August digs into the parish trust Isandro endowed: its income has quietly flowed to four founding families for fifty years, all justified by documents signed after his death. Whoever holds the death certificate holds the money. Emotional beat: understanding that the crime isn't murder but arithmetic.

chapters.title: Voices on Tape
chapters.summary: In the dispatch archive, August finds old answering-machine tapes Ruthie once left at the taxi office, begging for a ride to the cemetery — tapes someone paid to have destroyed, except one misfiled reel. On it, a man's voice says he will meet her below the church. Emotional beat: the dead speaking through machinery.

chapters.title: Below the Church
chapters.summary: August explores the flooded crypt at low water and finds a bricked side chamber, dry, furnished — someone lived here, recently. Cigarette ends, fresh oil on hinges. Isandro may have been alive within living memory. Emotional beat: vertigo as history refuses to stay buried.

chapters.title: The Heirs
chapters.summary: August maps the four founding families and their alibis across the three accidents. One heir, Judge Ambrose Pell, has lied about his whereabouts on every date. Another, young Tobias Vey, seems genuinely frightened — of his own family. Emotional beat: suspicion redistributing itself like weight.

chapters.title: Threats, Politely Delivered
chapters.summary: August's tires are slashed, then her landlord raises her rent overnight, then a patrol car idles outside her building. Cordelia calls to suggest August take a vacation. Emotional beat: pressure applied with white gloves, and August refusing to flinch.

chapters.title: Tobias Comes to the Office
chapters.summary: Tobias Vey appears at the dispatch desk at 3 a.m., confessing he was paid to burn the archivist's files and didn't know it would kill him. He gives August a key from his grandfather's effects, stamped with the crypt chamber's number. Emotional beat: a coward choosing, finally, a side.

chapters.title: The Key
chapters.summary: August returns to the crypt chamber and opens a locked strongbox: Isandro's own journal, describing how he staged his death to catch the trustees stealing, and naming Ruthie as his sole heir — which would dissolve the families' claim entirely. Emotional beat: the motive revealed, and its terrible price.

chapters.title: Ruthie Disappears
chapters.summary: Ruthie vanishes from the care facility the same night August decides to bring her forward. Sign-in sheets show a visitor matching Judge Pell. August realizes she led the family straight to the one living witness. Emotional beat: guilt as a physical weight, driving her faster.

chapters.title: The Viaduct
chapters.summary: Following Pell's pattern, August deduces Ruthie will be killed the same way as the others — a fall made to look accidental — and races to the viaduct where the first 'accident' happened. She arrives as Pell's fixer forces Ruthie toward the rail. Emotional beat: terror sharpened into action.

chapters.title: What Falls
chapters.summary: Climax begins. August intervenes; in the struggle the fixer falls instead, and Pell arrives expecting to manage a tidy scene — until he sees August recording everything on the old dispatch recorder, live-transmitting to the police band. Emotional beat: the hunter realizing the frequency was open all along.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Ruthie, shaking but upright, identifies herself publicly as Isandro's daughter at the courthouse steps, journal in hand. The trust freezes; warrants issue; Cordelia, unrepentant, tells August that towns run on convenient stories. Emotional beat: victory that tastes like ash and truth at once.

chapters.title: The Second Coffin
chapters.summary: Investigators reopen the crypt and find remains in the side chamber — not Isandro's, but the original sexton's, murdered in 1971 to protect the secret. Isandro himself died years ago in exile; only his plan survived him. Emotional beat: mourning a man she knew only through paper.

chapters.title: Burial, Corrected
chapters.summary: The town reburied what it actually buried, and Ruthie stands at the graveside as the crowd that ignored her for sixty years now applauds her. August watches from the back, uncomfortable with gratitude she didn't seek. Emotional beat: the strange loneliness of being right in public.

chapters.title: Dispatch
chapters.summary: August returns to the night shift, declining offers to consult or testify beyond necessity. A routine call comes in — a fare to the cemetery, again — and she listens differently now, knowing every voice carries a story someone wants unheard. Emotional beat: restored equilibrium, permanently recalibrated.

chapters.title: The Nameplate
chapters.summary: Final chapter, August's POV. She polishes the brass nameplate from the empty coffin, kept as a reminder, and files her notes on the three solved deaths beside the case that solved itself. Somewhere in Parish, another story waits. Emotional beat: quiet closure, and the promise of the next voice on the line.
